body_markdown:
For the second time in two years, the late Ayrton Senna’s 1991 Honda NSX is for sale. RM Sotheby’s has consigned the Japanese supercar to its October 31 London Auction, with a presale estimate of £500,000–£800,000 ($682K–$1.1M).


Ayrton Senna spent a fruitful six seasons racing for McLaren in Formula 1, where he won three World Drivers’ Championships, in 1988, 1990, and ’91. Honda provided the power for those titles, first with a turbocharged 1.5-liter V-6 and then a 3.5-liter V-10.


Throughout his career, Senna brought a deeply analytical mind to his race craft, which made him far more valuable to his teams than any mere driver, and the technical input he was able to provide his engineers was key to his success. It was also key to Honda’s development of the NSX.


Honda believed it had a winner on its hands when it unveiled the “New Sportscar eXperimental” in early 1989, but then Senna got behind the wheel and pooped on that party. The Brazilian informed the car’s engineers that the NSX felt fragile and lacked stiffness, and they listened. By the time he next drove one, they had stiffened the chassis by 50% and updated the suspension. The result was the near-perfect driver’s car that enthusiasts have lauded for 35 years now.


Honda gifted Senna three NSXs for personal use—two black ones and the car coming up for sale, chassis T000233, done in Formula Red with a black roof. He kept it in Portugal and used it whenever he was in the country at his property. He also commuted in it to the Estoril circuit for the 1991 Portuguese Grand Prix. The car appears in the documentary *Ayrton Senna: Racing Is in My Blood* .


Senna arrives at the Portuguese GP at Circuito Estoril on September 22, 1991.


Ercole Colombo/Studio Colombo/Getty Images


Following Senna’s death at Imola in 1994, the NSX has had a series of owners, and since[its 2024 sale](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/ayrton-sennas-nsx-could-be-yours/) for an undisclosed sum, it has been in Japan.


NSX values have been on a steady upward trajectory for the last 14 years, with average #2 (excellent) prices up nearly 250% in that time. And some sales in the last couple of years have delivered noteworthy results. In April 2025, Hagerty reported on a 2002 NSX-T result for a record $377,500. Little more than a month later, Broad Arrow sold a 2003 NSX-R, built for the Japanese market, at its Villa d’Este auction for[a staggering $1.06 million](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/2003-honda-nsx-r-tops-1m-and-breaks-record-at-villa-deste/) .


Courtesy Norio Koike


Both of those cars represented higher-performance models than a standard, early, 271-horsepower NSX like Senna’s, but two factors could significantly impact the value on sale day. First, and most obvious, is his well-documented ownership. Few F1 drivers have played so pivotal a role in developing a road car, and this one was his. And second is the year we are living in:[From the very start](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/sale-of-the-week/sotw-mecum-kissimmee-2026/) , 2026 has seen collectors go gaga in the supercar market, and given what we’ve just witnessed[in Monterey](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/2026-monterey-car-week-auctions-shatter-record-with-756m-in-sales/) , it would be unrealistic to think the whole thing could cool to absolute zero before the end of October. In fact, it would not surprise anyone around these parts if Ayrton Senna’s NSX sets a record in London. Watch this space…
